newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Europe, Islamic nations condemn Israel at U.N..
newsitem.headline: Europe, Islamic nations condemn Israel at U.N..

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
The European Union and Islamic nations criticised Israel on Thursday over the crisis with the Palestinians, calling on it to prove its commitment to the crumbling Middle East peace process.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali deplored the violence in the West Bank and Gaza, urging both sides to resume negotiations and implement existing agreements. The U.N. Security Council was expected to discuss the crisis later on Thursday as part of its regular consultations.
Twenty-nine Palestinians and five Israelis have been killed in two days of clashes.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, who speaks for the 15-nation bloc as his country currently holds the EU presidency, criticised Israel at a news conference on the margins of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.

EU foreign ministers discussed the latest Middle East crisis with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Wednesday and Ireland's Spring said he had also met Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy for talks.
Spring said he conveyed to Levy "our deepest concern in relation to the lack of momentum in the peace process."

"We emphasised very strongly and affirmatively the concern of the European Union that it was necessary for Israel to show ... a renewed commitment to the process ... signals need to be given by the Israeli government," he said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should maintain contacts with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to show the world that Israel would honour peace agreements reached between the two sides by the previous Israeli government.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said the U.N. Security Council would discuss the Middle East as part of regular consultations later on Thursday and that European countries wanted to send a clear message to Israel.
"It is necessary for Israel to give a signal, to take action that will demonstrate ... that Israel remains committed to peace," Dini told reporters.

"The disturbing fact ... is that in the Arab countries in the region the credibility of the Israeli government is being questioned and its commitment to peace, and that I think is dangerous and should not be allowed to continue."
Arab anger at Netanyahu's failure to extend self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza boiled over after his Likud government opened a tunnel near the al-Aqsa and Dome of the Rock mosques.

"Matters like that should be avoided in a situation which is particularly tense and fragile ... great care should be taken in terms of any action that could cause incidents and loss of life," Spring said.
Boutros-Ghali took a similar line in urging restraint.
His spokeswoman, Sylvana Foa, told reporters: "He deplores the escalation of violence... The Secretary-General urges restraint and appeals for a halt to any provocative action."
Boutros-Ghali called on both sides to end the violence and to "resume in earnest negotiations that will lead to full implementation of the agreements already reached."
Islamic nations also met to discuss the crisis.
"The hesitations of the Israeli government ... are paralysing (peace) efforts," Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC), told the meeting.
"The peace process is irreversible, it cannot be frozen. To question the agreements undertaken ... would be a dangerous precedent," he said.
Farouk Kaddoumi, foreign affairs spokesman for the Palestinians, told the OIC meeting Israel had abandoned the principle of "land for peace" in negotiations.
"The situation is deteriorating," he said."This is an inevitable outcome of the policy pursued by Israel."
